The programme is intended to support up to a 2-gigawatt buildout by 2027. The expansion focuses on adding land, power and data centre shell capacity at sites designed to host multiple generations of NVIDIA DSX systems. Participating providers will operate the facilities, while NVIDIA will supply the DSX platform, computing systems, networking, software and ecosystem support. Demand for AI computing has risen as companies, researchers and public sector bodies seek more local access to large-scale infrastructure for training and deploying models. The broader buildout is intended to serve Australian startups, universities, researchers, developers, enterprises and AI-focused companies. NVIDIA also tied the expansion to broader use of its Nemotron open models in Australia, saying greater local access to computing resources and models would help organisations develop regional applications and agents for domestic industries. **Partner buildout** Several participating groups also outlined separate projects under the wider programme. Firmus is extending its Project Southgate initiative, which is intended to support demand from hyperscale operators and AI-focused customers in Australia and the Asia-Pacific region. “Project Southgate represents a tangible commitment to building Australia's AI future,” said Oliver Curtis, Co-Founder and Co-CEO of Firmus. “Together with NVIDIA, we are developing AI factories that will give Australian businesses, researchers and innovators access to world-class computing capacity at home, while positioning Australia to meet growing AI demand across Asia-Pacific,” Curtis said. Sharon AI is deploying up to 68,000 NVIDIA GPUs linked with NVIDIA Quantum InfiniBand and NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet networking. The infrastructure is intended to support startups, enterprises and research organisations. “Australia has the energy, connectivity and ambition to lead in AI. That potential only becomes real capability when organizations can access world-class compute without compromising on security or sovereignty,” said James Manning, Co-Founder and CEO of Sharon AI. “By building on NVIDIA's DSX platform, Sharon AI is equipped to bring gigawatt-scale AI factories to Australian enterprises, researchers, government and AI natives. With the trust and reliability needed to build, train and deploy AI at scale, Australia can turn its natural advantages into a genuine national AI capability,” Manning said. IREN is combining NVIDIA's DSX architecture with its own operations across power, land, data centres and GPU deployment. highlights.content: [![Straitstimes.com header logo](/assets/ST-logo-default-aoeSLh4S.png)](https://www.straitstimes.com) # Are we losing control of AI? What’s driving new fears [Sign up now:](/newsletter-signup?ref=inline-article) Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox Top AI executives like Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei (left) and OpenAI chief Sam Altman (right) say they want to slow the breakneck pace of artificial intelligence development. PHOTOS: AFP Published Sep 15, 2026, 07:55 AM Updated Sep 15, 2026, 07:55 AM For years, as artificial intelligence (AI) has evolved from the stuff of science fiction movies to an app ordinary people have installed on their phones, tech leaders and some AI insiders have talked about the potential for it to escape human control and wreak havoc on society. Those fears have become impossible to ignore in recent days, driven by advances in the technology, a series of cybersecurity breaches involving AI agents, and new warnings from rank-and-file AI staff. Leading AI companies in the US have responded by suggesting they voluntarily slow their work to buy time to create safeguards. Some experts and officials say that is not good enough and are urging government restrictions. ## What sparked the current AI panic? The current AI panic was sparked by two developments – a startling cyberattack carried out by OpenAI models and a warning from a former Anthropic PBC and OpenAI employee about [the existential threat posed by advanced models](https://www.straitstimes.com/world/united-states/openai-ipo-will-not-happen-in-2026-amid-ai-safety-fears-chief-sam-altman-says?ref=inline-article). OpenAI said [a swarm of advanced AI agents inadvertently hacked Hugging Face,](https://www.straitstimes.com/world/openai-agents-hacked-hugging-face-in-700-strong-swarm-tried-to-cover-tracks-investigations?ref=inline-article) which hosts AI models and datasets, in an “unprecedented” incident in July. While operating in a “sandbox” testing environment – one designed to be isolated from the internet – OpenAI’s models exploited a vulnerability in the software of an unidentified third-party vendor to gain access to the internet and [ultimately breached Hugging Face’s infrastructure.](https://www.straitstimes.com/world/united-states/openai-agents-attacked-rubygems-before-hugging-face-incident-researchers-say?ref=inline-article) OpenAI said the models targeted Hugging Face’s database to gain access to secret information they could use for the evaluation. The incident caused widespread alarm about the ability of top AI firms to prevent and stop advanced AI models from operating outside their intended instructions. Hugging Face said the intrusion was “driven, end to end, by an autonomous AI agent system”. The OpenAI news prompted other companies to review their own security measures for testing advanced AI. Anthropic and Meta reported discovering previously unknown breaches. In late July, more than 1,000 staff across all the major AI companies signed a petition calling for a mechanism to slow the pace of AI development. After quitting his job at Anthropic, rank-and-file AI researcher Jacob Coxon, in a Sept 8 social media post, accused both the company and his former employer, OpenAI, of [“gambling with our lives”](https://www.straitstimes.com/world/united-states/theyre-playing-with-our-lives-ai-researcher-quits-anthropic?ref=inline-article) by “racing toward super-intelligent AI”. Coxon said the people building AI believe it could “kill us all by the end of the decade,” a point later echoed online by Anthropic employee Evan Hubinger. Hubinger said he believes there is a greater than 10 per cent chance that AI eliminates all humans in the next decade. Coxon’s posts have been viewed more than 170 million times on X as of Sept 14 and elicited [a flood of calls from policymakers](https://www.straitstimes.com/world/united-states/us-lawmakers-call-for-new-ai-rules-after-anthropic-researchers-safety-warnings?ref=inline-article) such as Senator Bernie Sa...

highlights.content: [](https://www.chosun.com/english) |[![Image 1](https://www.chosun.com/pf/resources/icons/eng-korea-icon.png?d=2372)](https://www.chosun.com/)[KOREAN](https://www.chosun.com/) [National](https://www.chosun.com/english/national-en/) [Market & Money](https://www.chosun.com/english/market-money-en/) [Industry](https://www.chosun.com/english/industry-en/) [North Korea](https://www.chosun.com/english/north-korea-en/) [Entertainment+](https://www.chosun.com/english/kpop-culture-en/) [Lifestyle](https://www.chosun.com/english/travel-food-en/) [World](https://www.chosun.com/english/world-en/) [Opinion](https://www.chosun.com/english/opinion-en/) [Sports](https://www.chosun.com/english/sports-en/) [English](https://www.chosun.com/english/)[Industry](https://www.chosun.com/english/industry-en/) # Z.AI Launches 35x Revenue Funding Round Company to allocate 60% of $5B to AI R&D and infrastructure [By Koo A-mo](https://www.chosun.com/english/people/koo-amo/) Published 2026.09.15. 00:34 ![Image 2: 중국 AI 스타트업 즈푸](https://www.chosun.com/resizer/v2/MQYGMZRRGE2TQZRWMRSWIYJVG4.jpg?auth=432d0a3d204fdd1bb40c1f75a1f622ad2e0f0efc91ae51001605049b1778e3c7&width=522&height=367&smart=true) Chinese AI startup Zi Pu Chinese AI startup Z.AI (Z.ai) has launched an additional funding round worth approximately 35 times its first-half revenue this year. While its sales are growing rapidly, the company struggles to cover costs for next-generation model development and computing expenses solely through its own revenue. According to a September 13 report by the Hong Kong-based South China Morning Post (SCMP), Z.AI disclosed to the Hong Kong Stock Exchange that it plans to raise $2 billion (approximately 2.7 trillion Korean won) through new share issuance and $3 billion (approximately 4 trillion Korean won) via convertible bonds. In July, Z.AI had already secured 31.4 billion Hong Kong dollars (approximately 5.4 trillion Korean won) through stock sales. Z.AI intends to allocate approximately 60% of the newly raised funds to research and development of next-generation models and a "fully autonomous learning" system. This includes building computing infrastructure for large-scale model training and inference, compatibility work with domestically produced semiconductors, and improving inference efficiency. Founded in 2019 by researchers from Tsinghua University, Z.AI listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange in January. From February to August this year, it upgraded its in-house large language model (LLM) series "GLM" at roughly two-month intervals. Continuous model development and upgrades require significant costs. Z.AI’s first-half revenue this year surged 400% year-on-year to 953.89 million Chinese yuan (approximately 190.8 billion Korean won). However, its R&D expenses reached 2.13 billion Chinese yuan (approximately 426 billion Korean won), 2.2 times its revenue, with losses amounting to 2.07 billion Chinese yuan (approximately 414 billion Korean won). As of the end of June, the company held 3.99 billion Chinese yuan (approximately 798 billion Korean won) in cash. AI models are not one-time products. Training new models requires massive GPU resources, data, and manpower, while inference costs for generating user responses continue post-launch. If competitors enhance performance, immediate development of the next model becomes necessary. Even as customers and sales grow, computing costs rise accordingly. Other Chinese AI firms are also competing to secure funding. highlights.content: Posted: # AI infrastructure company Cornelis raises $205M to chip away at Nvidia’s dominance Cornelis, a company creating networking technology to help AI chips communicate more effectively, announced Monday that it has raised $205 million in a funding round led by IAG Capital Partners. It also announced a product called Active Compute Fabric, a network technology that targets the fact that much GPU time is wasted waiting for data to arrive. Cornelis hopes to address this with a networking fabric that lets chips process and send information at the same time. The company, which spun off from Intel in 2020, is competing with Nvidia by offering an open architecture, meaning customers can use a variety of GPU and accelerator hardware with Cornelis’ networking fabric. Though Nvidia chips can technically run on other networking fabrics, they’re optimized to run on Nvidia’s own software, making it much easier — and more enticing — for customers to use Nvidia’s full GPU stack. Cornelis is part of a new wave of AI infrastructure companies emerging to break apart Nvidia’s market dominance, piece by piece (or chip by chip, one could say). Cornelis has already started shipping its product and is working on a new generation of it, expected to be released later this year. Last day to book an exhibit table is September 18. Manoher Bommena, a Vice President of Engineering at semiconductor firm Renesas, said "Cognichip's ACI represents one of the most comprehensive approaches to bringing AI into the contemporary design environment – it simply 'speaks chip'". Early results point to a roughly 100 times speedup of chip design, with lower power, higher performance, and lower chip cost. What’s driving new fears [Sign up now:](/newsletter-signup?ref=inline-article) Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox Top AI executives like Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei (left) and OpenAI chief Sam Altman (right) say they want to slow the breakneck pace of artificial intelligence development. PHOTOS: AFP Published Sep 15, 2026, 07:55 AM Updated Sep 15, 2026, 07:55 AM For years, as artificial intelligence (AI) has evolved from the stuff of science fiction movies to an app ordinary people have installed on their phones, tech leaders and some AI insiders have talked about the potential for it to escape human control and wreak havoc on society. Those fears have become impossible to ignore in recent days, driven by advances in the technology, a series of cybersecurity breaches involving AI agents, and new warnings from rank-and-file AI staff. Leading AI companies in the US have responded by suggesting they voluntarily slow their work to buy time to create safeguards. Some experts and officials say that is not good enough and are urging government restrictions. ## What sparked the current AI panic? The current AI panic was sparked by two developments – a startling cyberattack carried out by OpenAI models and a warning from a former Anthropic PBC and OpenAI employee about [the existential threat posed by advanced models](https://www.straitstimes.com/world/united-states/openai-ipo-will-not-happen-in-2026-amid-ai-safety-fears-chief-sam-altman-says?ref=inline-article). OpenAI said [a swarm of advanced AI agents inadvertently hacked Hugging Face,](https://www.straitstimes.com/world/openai-agents-hacked-hugging-face-in-700-strong-swarm-tried-to-cover-tracks-investigations?ref=inline-article) which hosts AI models and datasets, in an “unprecedented” incident in July. While operating in a “sandbox” testing environment – one designed to be isolated from the internet – OpenAI’s models exploited a vulnerability in the software of an unidentified third-party vendor to gain access to the internet and [ultimately breached Hugging Face’s infrastructure.](https://www.straitstimes.com/world/united-states/openai-agents-attacked-rubygems-before-hugging-face-incident-researchers-say?ref=inline-article) OpenAI said the models targeted Hugging Face’s database to gain access to secret information they could use for the evaluation. The incident caused widespread alarm about the ability of top AI firms to prevent and stop advanced AI models from operating outside their intended instructions. Hugging Face said the intrusion was “driven, end to end, by an autonomous AI agent system”. The OpenAI news prompted other companies to review their own security measures for testing advanced AI. Anthropic and Meta reported discovering previously unknown breaches. In late July, more than 1,000 staff across all the major AI companies signed a petition calling for a mechanism to slow the pace of AI development. After quitting his job at Anthropic, rank-and-file AI researcher Jacob Coxon, in a Sept 8 social media post, accused both the company and his former employer, OpenAI, of [“gambling with our lives”](https://www.straitstimes.com/world/united-states/theyre-playing-with-our-lives-ai-researcher-quits-anthropic?ref=inline-article) by “racing toward super-intelligent AI”. Coxon said the people building AI believe it could “kill us all by the end of the decade,” a point later echoed online by Anthropic employee Evan Hubinger. Hubinger said he believes there is a greater than 10 per cent chance that AI eliminates all humans in the next decade. Coxon’s posts have been viewed more than 170 million times on X as of Sept 14 and elicited [a flood of calls from policymakers](https://www.straitstimes.com/world/united-states/us-lawmakers-call-for-new-ai-rules-after-anthropic-researchers-safety-warnings?ref=inline-article) such as Senator Bernie Sa...

The oversubscribed Series A was led by Singapore-based [Serendipity Capital](https://app.thequantuminsider.com/investor/44a3bb62-ef96-490e-abcf-faf22f7eb193/profile), according to the company. Other participants included TEL Venture Capital, the corporate venture arm of Japanese chip-equipment maker [Tokyo Electron](https://app.thequantuminsider.com/company/7f477028-7935-4b97-8eaa-1b5ed674193b/profile), and investors connected to manufacturing, defense, quantum computing and critical infrastructure. Update your preferences in [Account Settings](/account/preferences/) ![](https://static.time.com/v3/assets/bltea6093859af6183b/blt2df29e3f0391590f/6aa77407f65bda8366023fcf/AI-Questions-Revolution.jpg?branch=production&width=3840&quality=75&auto=webp&crop=3:2) Personalized Content ## Paula Goldman Follow this author to personalize your feed and get instant alerts. WHY FOLLOW? Update your preferences in [Account Settings](/account/preferences/) In just a few years, AI has gone from a specialist topic to something everyone has opinions on. It has been praised as miraculous, condemned as dangerous, and debated everywhere from boardrooms to dinner tables. But between these poles of euphoria and dread lies the reality most of us now face: a technology powerful enough to reshape how work gets done, yet still deeply dependent on human judgment. Too often, headlines focus on extremes, but the practical questions are far more grounded. How do we manage this technology? How do we and our teams work alongside it effectively? How do we capture its benefits without compromising our values or our goals? To find useful answers, we have to start by understanding where we are, what has truly changed, and what has not. Artificial intelligence, after all, is not new. It has been with us since [at least 1956](https://time.com/7340901/ai-history-bubble-benchmarks/), when a small group of computer scientists gathered at Dartmouth College to explore a deceptively simple [question](https://time.com/archive/6728762/can-machines-think/): Can machines think? Since then, the technology has seen decades of progress and setbacks, so-called AI summers and winters. AI didn’t suddenly appear in the world in the 2020s. But powerful, general-purpose AI systems pushed the technology into mainstream awareness in ways that earlier breakthroughs never did. It’s natural that the reactions have been polarized; rapid change often leaves people unsure what comes next. Today’s systems are powerful and raise new challenges, and we will take those challenges seriously throughout this book. But they are not as alien or unmanageable as they are sometimes made out to be. We already have decades of lessons and frameworks from earlier generations of AI and from other complex technologies, from aviation to automobiles to power plants, all of which can be adapted to this moment. Advertisement Understanding what’s the same and what’s different about this moment for AI and work, and how we can build on what we already know, is crucial. If you’re new to AI, I will offer you a map of essential concepts so you can navigate confidently. If you’ve been here for a while, I will reframe the challenge, moving the conversation toward leadership and collaboration rather than technical mastery alone. It has been praised as miraculous, condemned as dangerous, and debated everywhere from boardrooms to dinner tables. But between these poles of euphoria and dread lies the reality most of us now face: a technology powerful enough to reshape how work gets done, yet still deeply dependent on human judgment. Too often, headlines focus on extremes, but the practical questions are far more grounded. How do we manage this technology? How do we and our teams work alongside it effectively? How do we capture its benefits without compromising our values or our goals? To find useful answers, we have to start by understanding where we are, what has truly changed, and what has not. Artificial intelligence, after all, is not new. But powerful, general-purpose AI systems pushed the technology into mainstream awareness in ways that earlier breakthroughs never did. It’s natural that the reactions have been polarized; rapid change often leaves people unsure what comes next. Today’s systems are powerful and raise new challenges, and we will take those challenges seriously throughout this book. But they are not as alien or unmanageable as they are sometimes made out to be. While its sales are growing rapidly, the company struggles to cover costs for next-generation model development and computing expenses solely through its own revenue. According to a September 13 report by the Hong Kong-based South China Morning Post (SCMP), Z.AI disclosed to the Hong Kong Stock Exchange that it plans to raise $2 billion (approximately 2.7 trillion Korean won) through new share issuance and $3 billion (approximately 4 trillion Korean won) via convertible bonds. In July, Z.AI had already secured 31.4 billion Hong Kong dollars (approximately 5.4 trillion Korean won) through stock sales. Z.AI intends to allocate approximately 60% of the newly raised funds to research and development of next-generation models and a "fully autonomous learning" system. This includes building computing infrastructure for large-scale model training and inference, compatibility work with domestically produced semiconductors, and improving inference efficiency. Founded in 2019 by researchers from Tsinghua University, Z.AI listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange in January. From February to August this year, it upgraded its in-house large language model (LLM) series "GLM" at roughly two-month intervals. Continuous model development and upgrades require significant costs. Z.AI’s first-half revenue this year surged 400% year-on-year to 953.89 million Chinese yuan (approximately 190.8 billion Korean won). However, its R&D expenses reached 2.13 billion Chinese yuan (approximately 426 billion Korean won), 2.2 times its revenue, with losses amounting to 2.07 billion Chinese yuan (approximately 414 billion Korean won). As of the end of June, the company held 3.99 billion Chinese yuan (approximately 798 billion Korean won) in cash. AI models are not one-time products. Training new models requires massive GPU resources, data, and manpower, while inference costs for generating user responses continue post-launch. If competitors enhance performance, immediate development of the next model becomes necessary. Even as customers and sales grow, computing costs rise accordingly. Other Chinese AI firms are also competing to secure funding. As I described in [a recent article](https://www.forbes.com/sites/karlfreund/2026/08/03/could-eda-ai-startups-be-the-new-claude-of-chip-design/), several chip design startups are working to revolutionize chip design with AI, just as Anthropic's Claude Code has revolutionized software development. Could we be approaching the day when AI can design a finished chip just from the specifications? With Cognichip's AI Chip Intelligence (ACI) announcement, we just took a huge step in that direction. Instead of using agentic AI and Large Language Models (LLMs), Cognichip took a unique approach and developed physics-based AI models to automate each step in chip design. Details will be presented at this week's AI Infra Summit being held in Santa Clara. How good is this new approach? Manoher Bommena, a Vice President of Engineering at semiconductor firm Renesas, said "Cognichip's ACI represents one of the most comprehensive approaches to bringing AI into the contemporary design environment – it simply 'speaks chip'". Early results point to a roughly 100 times speedup of chip design, with lower power, higher performance, and lower chip cost. The company has raised $93 million in total funding from Mayfield Fund, Lux Capital, FPV Ventures, Seligman Ventures, SBI Investment, and Candou Ventures. Let's dive in. ## The Cognichip ACI Full-Stack Design System Most chip design AI tools today are based either on reinforcement learning, such as physical layout tools, or a wrapper around a Large Language Model (LLM), which are trained on a massive amount of text and a relatively small sample of chip design data. One reason we haven't seen a model trained on chip design is the lack of available data for training such a model. Chip design details are notoriously well-kept secrets, so there simply isn't enough public data to train a neural network adequately. Cognichip made a strategic bet and built their foundation models on the experiences of its own design team and synthetic data, taking the data sparsity challenge in semiconductors head-on. ![Instead of wrapping AI around EDA tools, Cognichip built its platform from the ground up on AI.](https://s.yimg.com/lo/mysterio/api/dc81a0c6412821703b8308503048a9273d54b9060c99078de9f7938a3d93c392/lightyear_networkapi/resizefill_w959_h494%3Bquality_80%3Bformat_webp/https%3A%2F%2Fmedia.zenfs.com%2Fen%2Fforbes_contributor_845%2Fdadeeae07f51c4bbe39397c4605ea38e.png) Instead of wrapping AI around EDA tools, Cognichip built its platform from the ground up on AI. Newsletter](#boxzilla-138215) # Why DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash Is Such an Exciting Open Model Release DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash shows how Causal Encoder-Decoder architecture, MoE, KV cache compression, CSA2, cheaper prefill, and efficient decoding can make powerful open-source AI models far more efficient to run. By **[Abid Ali Awan](https://www.kdnuggets.com/author/abidali-awan)**, KDnuggets Assistant Editor on September 14, 2026 in [Language Models](https://www.kdnuggets.com/tag/language-models) --- DeepSeek has released **DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash**, and while the benchmark numbers are impressive, they are probably not the most interesting part of this release. The architecture is. What Current Research Really Shows ![Suyash Raizada](/blog-media/authors/QHoc5VfTtKij/avatar.jpg) ![Can AI Train AI Models Without Humans? What Current Research Really Shows](/_next/image/?url=%2Fblog-media%2Fposts%2F8dbe81ef-f76%2Fcan-ai-train-ai-models-without-humans-what-current-research-really-shows.jpg&w=1920&q=75) **Can AI train AI models without humans?** Yes, in narrow and increasingly impressive ways. AI systems can now generate tasks, label data, score answers, create synthetic datasets, and run self-play loops that improve model behavior with little day-to-day human input. But fully human-free training of the next generation of frontier AI models is not ready for safe, general deployment. Humans still set the goals, write the rules, choose architectures, control compute, and decide what is acceptable in the real world. Anyone trying to build a working understanding of this space often starts with a structured credential like the [**Certified Artificial Intelligence (AI) Expert**](https://www.blockchain-council.org/certifications/certified-artificial-intelligence-ai-expert/), which lays out where automation genuinely helps and where human judgment is still required. That distinction matters. A model can teach itself to solve coding puzzles. It cannot, by itself, decide what a hospital chatbot should refuse, what a legal assistant should cite, or when a self-improving agent should be stopped. ![Certified Artificial Intelligence Expert Ad Strip](/blog-ads/email-strip/certified-agentic-ai-expert.png) ## What Does "AI Training AI" Actually Mean? When researchers talk about AI training AI, they usually mean models are taking over parts of the training pipeline that humans used to do by hand. Those parts include: Generating prompts, tasks, and examples Creating synthetic data for training Producing labels for unlabeled data Scoring model answers as a reward signal Selecting harder examples as the model improves Critiquing unsafe or low-quality outputs This is not science fiction. It already happens in modern machine learning teams. A common workflow uses a stronger model to label thousands or millions of examples, then trains a smaller model on that output. Another lets a reasoning model generate coding or math problems, solve them, validate the answers with a tool such as Python, and train on the successful attempts. Practitioners looking to move from reading about these pipelines to actually building them often pursue the [**Certified Artificial Intelligence (AI) Developer**](https://www.blockchain-council.org/certifications/certified-artificial-intelligence-ai-developer/) track, which focuses on hands-on implementation rather than theory alone. There is still a hidden human layer underneath. People decide the loss function, the benchmark, the safety policy, the deployment environment, and the point at which a model is good enough to ship. ## The Main Ways AI Trains Other AI Models ### Self-Supervised Learning and Pseudo-Labeling Self-supervised learning is the foundation of most large language models. The model learns from raw text by predicting missing or next tokens, without a person labeling each sentence. Pseudo-labeling takes this further. A trained model generates labels for unlabeled data, filters the most confident ones, and uses them to train a new model. MIT researchers have explored fast self-training, where a pre-trained model labels raw data, keeps high-confidence predictions, and retrains iteratively. This cuts the need for manual annotation, especially in domains where labels are costly. A practical warning: confidence filtering is not magic. LLMs.titleZh: Does AI Have Low EQ? USC Study Identifies Where Models’ Emotional Reasoning Breaks Down
LLMs.content: [![Image](https://viterbischool.usc.edu/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/USC-Shield-BlackBG.png)](https://usc.edu/) [![Formal](https://viterbischool.usc.edu/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Formal-Viterbi-Logo-New.png)](/) --- [School of Engineering](/) # Does AI Have Low EQ? USC Study Identifies Where Models’ Emotional Reasoning Breaks Down Venice Tang | September 14, 2026  USC Viterbi and USC Stevens engineers reveal how AI models misinterpret emotional cues from audio and video, and introduce a framework to help them reason with real evidence ![Illustration of a robot staring at a red heart. (Credit: Midjourney)](https://viterbischool.usc.edu/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/1200-x-600-article-feature-photos-23.png) AI emotional reasoning through audios and videos (Credit: Midjourney) Have you ever interacted with an AI-powered customer support agent only to find it strangely nonempathetic, cold, disconnected and unable to understand how you’re feeling? Unlike humans, AI does not actually experience emotions. Instead, it can appear to understand emotions by using logic to infer them from audio and visual cues — a capability known as emotion reasoning. This ability is often found in multimodal large language models (MLLMs), advanced AI systems that can understand and analyze multiple types of data, like images, audio, video and text, simultaneously. However, today’s AI technologies still face significant limitations in emotion reasoning, often hallucinating or completely mislabeling how people feel. These errors can compromise the reliability of AI agents in social interactions and other complex emotion reasoning scenarios. USC researcher [Mohammad Soleymani](https://viterbi.usc.edu/directory/faculty/Soleymani/Mohammad) led a study investigating why AI models fail to associate audiovisual cues with the correct emotions and how to “debug AI’s logic” by proposing a new optimization framework that helps ensure emotional judgments are logically grounded in actual evidence. The project, which began last spring, resulted in the paper, “[AVERE: Improving Audiovisual Emotion Reasoning With Preference Optimization](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.07054),” which was accepted to the [International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR) 2026](https://iclr.cc/Conferences/2026/index.html). The study was funded by the [Army Research Office (ARO)](https://arl.devcom.army.mil/who-we-are/aro/), the [National Science Foundation (NSF)](https://www.nsf.gov/) and the [National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH)](https://www.nimh.nih.gov/). The research team also included Soleymani’s PhD students Jiacheng Pang and Ashutosh Chaubey, as well as Maksim Siniukov. Soleymani is a research associate professor at [USC Viterbi School of Engineering](https://viterbi.usc.edu/) and the [USC Mark and Mary Stevens School of Computing and AI](https://stevens-computing-ai.usc.edu/)‘s [Thomas Lord Department of Computer Science](https://www.cs.usc.edu/), he is also a research scientist at the [USC Institute for Creative Technologies](https://ict.usc.edu/). ## How Does AI Think About Emotions: Designing an EQ Test for AI “Our first step was to understand and quantify these challenges and pinpoint where and how exactly these multimodal models fail in the emotion reasoning process,” explained Soleymani. The team extracted video clips and created a benchmark called EmoReAlM that consists of 4,000 multiple-choice questions. AI models are given videos along with separate audio and visual captions and asked questions to correctly identify the emotions present in the clips and the evidence behind their answers. The researchers emphasized that this benchmark was a crucial step forward because previous studies had not systematically evaluated the failure modes of MLLMs. ## AI Can Be (Selectively) Blind and Deaf Soleymani’s team identified two categories of AI mistakes, or failure modes: reasoning errors and perception errors. They found that reasoning errors occur when a model correctly ide...

Findings of ILTA’s Tech Survey May Surprise You](https://www.lawnext.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/ILTA-2026-Survey-Cover.png) By [Bob Ambrogi](https://www.lawnext.com/author/ambrogi) on Tweet ![twitter]() Share ![linkedin]() Share ![facebook]() At the recent conference of the International Legal Technology Association, the big legal AI vendors CoCounsel, Harvey and Legora had outsized presences, with ginormous booths in the exhibit hall, major-name performers at their parties, and advertising so ubiquitous it even popped up in people’s Uber apps. (See: [Have We Reached ‘Peak Legal Tech?’ Sure Felt That Way At ILTACON this Week](https://www.lawnext.com/2026/08/have-we-reached-peak-legal-tech-sure-felt-that-way-at-iltacon-this-week.html).) So which of those is the preferred choice of law firms? Turns out, the answer is “None of the above,” at least according to the findings of the [just released 2026 technology survey](https://www.iltanet.org/resources/publications/surveys/ts26). The survey spanned over 500 law firms — all ILTA members — from small boutiques to global giants, representing a dozen countries and 140,000 lawyers. Of them, the vast majority, 94%, say they are using or exploring generative AI tools, up from 80% last year. But when ILTA asked the firms which tool they are using or exploring, the leader by a wide margin was Microsoft 365 Copilot, used by 76% of firms. Second place was effectively a three-way tie between two of the leading legal AI products, Thomson Reuters CoCounsel (44%) and Harvey (43%), and one non-legal general AI product, Anthropic’s Claude (44%). Legora came in much lower in the results, at 16%, behind products such as Lexis+AI (26%), ChatGPT Enterprise (22%), iManage (22%) and Litera One (17%). Breaking that down by firm size shows interesting patterns. Among firms of fewer than 50 lawyers, Copilot retains its top position (59%), followed again by Claude (42%) and CoCounsel (40%), but Harvey drops to 22% and Legora to 6%. At the other end of the size spectrum, among firms of 700 or more lawyers, the gap narrows between Copilot and Harvey, with Copilot seeing usage among 88% of firms and Harvey among 84%. But even among those large firms, Claude still gets 64% of usage, ahead of Legora (47%) and CoCounsel (43%). ### Deployment vs. Piloting It is one thing for a firm to say it is using one or more of these AI products, but it is another thing entirely to consider where these firms are in their AI deployment. Here again, the survey offers some revealing data. Only two AI products in the survey have been fully deployed by at least half of respondent firms’ lawyers: Microsoft Copilot, with 52% of firms reporting full deployment among lawyers, and Westlaw Advantage, with 50% of firms reporting full deployment. However, here is where the survey results get a bit confusing, as the Copilot that leads in deployment is not Microsoft 365 Copilot, which is a paid product, but, as the survey puts it, “Microsoft Copilot (formerly Bing Chat),” which would appear to be the free version included in Windows. AI Product.titleZh: A Vinyl Bar in Shibuya is a startup from a former Spotify leader for making music apps | TechCrunch
AI Product.content: As AI rages on, new startups are creating tools for people to create music using generative AI prompts in the style of any artist they want. A Vinyl Bar in Shibuya, a startup that sounds more like an indie band name, is focused on releasing a series of small apps that let you play around with sounds and vocals. The company has raised a $5.5m pre-seed round from Mantis VC, SV Angel, Boxgroup, Quiet Capital, Remarkable Ventures, Common Metal, Gold House, Liquid 2 Ventures, Breakers VC, Collaborative Fund, Systemic Ventures, and former Spotify chief content and advertising business officer, Dawn Ostroff, who joined the company as an advisor. The startup is built by Máuhan M Zonoozy, who was the former head of innovation at Spotify. Prior to that, he founded a video clipping and remixing startup called Bubbl, which was acquired by Cricket Media. Zonoozy, who left Spotify in 2024, said that he always wanted to go back to building something of his own. He thought that while streaming solved the access problem, most of the interaction with music was still around consumption. “I think when I looked at emergent behaviors and younger audiences, like everyone’s growing up playing with culture through games, through filters, through creation tools. And I just felt like there was an opportunity to empower people to do something similar with music,” he told TechCrunch. The startup releases these experiments like “singles” that are part of an album. The common theme between all of these apps or websites is interacting with different elements to create music or modify sound. For instance, Speed Surfer is a Chrome extension that changes the speed and filter of sound playing in your browser window. Usersound is a website where you can create an “audio” username with each letter representing a note. Stacks is a stem player where you can create mixes by turning bars on or off in a 3×3 grid. Drops is about placing plaques in a pattern to deflect marbles falling down, which creates musical notes. Sampler is a website that turns YouTube videos into music samplers based on beats of different parts of the songs. The company’s more ambitious product is an iOS app called bop. This lets you place musical instruments and effects in a grid to create different mixes of a base song. You can also adjust tempo and add one-time effects. Once you create these mixes, you can easily export them to TikTok or Instagram. A Vinyl Bar in Shibuya is also working on a multiplayer version, which would let users remix songs with others. The company recently added a prompt-based feature to create a sound. Zonoozy said that it is making an informed choice not to infuse AI into every part of these apps. He is open to using AI to build these products and to make infrastructure solid, though. “AI is obviously extraordinarily powerful, but I think we just don’t necessarily believe that the future of music is simply generation, like song generation via AI. And I think if AI starts to make that content more abundant, it actually makes taste and human perspective and interaction and participation even more important and even more valuable. And we’re just trying to make sure it doesn’t make it even rarer,” he said. This year, the company aims to release a “musical sandbox mixer” product that would let users play around with different elements of music-making, including being able to create instruments. The story title was changed because, at the time of testing last month, there were no prompt-based features in the startup’s apps. The company added prompt-based features more recently to its apps. The company has raised a $5.5m pre-seed round from Mantis VC, SV Angel, Boxgroup, Quiet Capital, Remarkable Ventures, Common Metal, Gold House, Liquid 2 Ventures, Breakers VC, Collaborative Fund, Systemic Ventures, and former Spotify chief content and advertising business officer, Dawn Ostroff, who joined the company as an advisor. The startup is built by Máuhan M Zonoozy, who was the former head of innovation at Spotify. Prior to that, he founded a video clipping and remixing startup called Bubbl, which was acquired by Cricket Media. Zonoozy, who left Spotify in 2024, said that he always wanted to go back to building something of his own. He thought that while streaming solved the access problem, most of the interaction with music was still around consumption. “I think when I looked at emergent behaviors and younger audiences, like everyone’s growing up playing with culture through games, through filters, through creation tools. And I just felt like there was an opportunity to empower people to do something similar with music,” he told TechCrunch. The startup releases these experiments like “singles” that are part of an album. The common theme between all of these apps or websites is interacting with different elements to create music or modify sound. For instance, Speed Surfer is a Chrome extension that changes the speed and filter of sound playing in your browser window. Usersound is a website where you can create an “audio” username with each letter representing a note. Stacks is a stem player where you can create mixes by turning bars on or off in a 3×3 grid. Drops is about placing plaques in a pattern to deflect marbles falling down, which creates musical notes. Sampler is a website that turns YouTube videos into music samplers based on beats of different parts of the songs. The company’s more ambitious product is an iOS app called bop. This lets you place musical instruments and effects in a grid to create different mixes of a base song. You can also adjust tempo and add one-time effects. Once you create these mixes, you can easily export them to TikTok or Instagram. A Vinyl Bar in Shibuya is also working on a multiplayer version, which would let users remix songs with others. The company recently added a prompt-based feature to create a sound. Zonoozy said that it is making an informed choice not to infuse AI into every part of these apps. He is open to using AI to build these products and to make infrastructure solid, though. “AI is obviously extraordinarily powerful, but I think we just don’t necessarily believe that the future of music is simply generation, like song generation via AI. And I think if AI starts to make that content more abundant, it actually makes taste and human perspective and interaction and participation even more important and even more valuable. And we’re just trying to make sure it doesn’t make it even rarer,” he said. This year, the company aims to release a “musical sandbox mixer” product that would let users play around with different elements of music-making, including being able to create instruments. The story title was changed because, at the time of testing last month, there were no prompt-based features in the startup’s apps. The company added prompt-based features more recently to its apps. MCP’s usage has grown at an astonishing rate. Across MCP’s Tier 1 SDKs, monthly downloads are approaching half a billion, with both the TypeScript and Python SDKs surpassing 1 billion downloads total. Usage in production is climbing just as fast. MCP tool calls from ChatGPT users reached 98 times their January level by August, and Resend passed one million MCP calls in a single month. That scale is exactly why a common way to validate MCP expertise is needed. The MCPA provides engineers, platform teams, and AI governance professionals a way to demonstrate their understanding of how the protocol works, how its components interact, and how to apply it responsibly. ![](https://www.hpcwire.com/aiwire/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2026/05/Agentic-AI-Foundation-AAIF-300x157.jpg) “We built MCP so developers could rely on one open protocol instead of writing custom integrations for every system. Since then, it has grown exponentially. Candidates are tested on MCP hosts, clients, servers, and tools; message flow and protocol primitives; trust boundaries, permissions, and risk controls; and how MCP is applied across real-world agentic deployments. The certification is aligned with the latest MCP specification release, [2026-07-28](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28), and is recommended for candidates who understand the internals of the MCP and are comfortable reasoning about how the protocol works and how its components communicate. “MCP has quickly become the standard for connecting AI agents to external systems. Open Source AI.content: # OpenHunterAI releases an AI red-team engine after killing the startup **The local-first alpha tests web, API and LLM apps, while its noncommercial license preserves a route back to paid software.** By [Ryan Merket](/author/ryan-merket) · Published Primary source: [X - Nicolas Krassas](https://x.com/Dinosn/status/2099505079048945883) ## Why it matters OpenHunterAI shows one path for abandoned AI startups: release the core product for distribution, retain commercial rights and let adoption test whether a business remains. [Nicolas Krassas (@Dinosn)](https://x.com/Dinosn) said [in a post on X](https://x.com/Dinosn/status/2099505079048945883) on September 14th that his group had abandoned plans for an AI security startup and released its red-team engine as [OpenHunterAI](https://github.com/LumosLab-Innovation/OpenHunterAI). "We killed the startup idea and released the red-team engine instead," Krassas wrote. The decision puts the code in developers' hands while preserving the option to charge for commercial use, a narrower bet than building and selling another hosted security platform from scratch. Krassas brings an operator's background to that decision. His [public profile](https://ch.linkedin.com/in/nicolas-krassas) lists threat and vulnerability management work at Henkel, penetration testing and security leadership roles, along with earlier work securing the official Athens 2004 Olympics website. He also studied neural networks at the University of Leeds, giving the project a technical lineage that predates the current rush to attach language models to application-security scanners. OpenHunterAI runs on a user's machine through Docker Compose and is designed to assess verified public websites, APIs and LLM applications. Users define a target, verify its domain, authorize a scope and approve a scan plan before workers begin testing. The interface collects scan activity, evidence, findings, remediation guidance and manual retests in one local workspace. The product combines browser inspection, reconnaissance, OWASP ZAP and an adapter for the Nuclei vulnerability scanner. AI models assist with triage, attack hypotheses and remediation guidance. Users supply their own model-provider credentials, and the documentation cautions that local hosting does not make the system fully offline: requests can still reach external model providers and the target under assessment. OpenHunterAI also includes a skill that lets coding agents prepare assessments from inside an application repository. The published installation command names Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI and Grok Build as supported clients. The skill starts with a read-only helper and requires human approval before a scan begins. ### The release is an alpha, with blockers documented in the repo The public repository is unusually direct about what remains unfinished. Its [release-readiness review](https://github.com/LumosLab-Innovation/OpenHunterAI/blob/main/docs/PUBLIC_RELEASE_READINESS.md) labels OpenHunterAI an alpha and says the review covers source code rather than evidence from a fresh production deployment or a complete target scan. One blocker concerns Nuclei. OpenHunterAI packages an adapter, but the reviewed template bundle and its configuration are incomplete. The review warns that process errors can appear as an empty successful result because one execution path parses output without fully handling the underlying process failure. OpenHunterAI's own documentation tells users to resolve that blocker before scanning. OpenHack and Strix, two other security runtimes referenced by the project, must also be installed separately. The readiness review calls for a complete authorized end-to-end scan, including callbacks, reports, exports and manual retesting, after the blockers are fixed. It also says the PDF export truncates long reports, making JSON, DOCX or HTML the safer formats for complete output. Those caveats matter for a tool that can otherwise produce the appearance of s...

He also proposed that AI corporations allow access by third-party evaluators and pursue international cooperation. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis, and Tesla CEO Elon Musk echoed Amodei's argument, bringing the call to slow AI to the forefront. ◇ Two leaders effectively reject calls to slow AI But the president of the United States, home to these big tech corporations, appears unwilling to slow the pace of AI development. On the 14th (local time), President Trump used the social media platform Truth Social to criticize recent calls by big tech leaders to slow AI as a "deranged conspiracy theory and a scam." He added, "The only control or guardrails needed for AI are a strong and smart president," and said, "The United States has exactly such a president." He continued to post criticisms of slowing AI, saying, for example, "The only reason for the AI and data center boom is that the United States is far ahead of every other country. Frankly, I want to keep it that way, because whoever wins in AI wins." Within a day, he ratcheted up his criticism of the call to slow AI. Infra & Chips.content: TelcoNews Australia - Telecommunications news for ICT decision-makers [![TelcoNews Australia logo](/brands/tn-new-logo.svg)](/) [Powered By ![TechDay logo](/brands/td-new-logo-right.svg)](https://techday.com.au) ![NVIDIA expands Australian AI infrastructure with partners](https://telconews.com.au/uploads/story/2026/09/14/neutral-australian-data-center-server-rows-network-lines-startup-laptop-university-office-modern-digital-illustration-story-318936.webp) [Cloud Security](https://telconews.com.au/tag/cloud-security) [Edge Computing](https://telconews.com.au/tag/edge-computing) [DC](https://telconews.com.au/tag/data-centers) # NVIDIA expands Australian AI infrastructure with partners Mon, 14th Sep 2026 (Today) [![Sean Mitchell](https://telconews.com.au/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6MTYyOSwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--a929a91c2a04d9af95ed98b14ed4d405bc70c1a7/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6eyJmb3JtYXQiOiJ3ZWJwIiwicmVzaXplX3RvX2ZpbGwiOlsxNjAsMTYwXSwicXVhbGl0eSI6ODV9LCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--89ddf5e6765c65a563c2258053e9d33c05d195da/IMG_3092.webp) SEAN MITCHELL Publisher](/author/sean-mitchell) NVIDIA has expanded its Australian AI infrastructure partnerships with Firmus, Sharon AI, IREN, Megaport, ResetData, CDC, NEXTDC and AirTrunk. The programme is intended to support up to a 2-gigawatt buildout by 2027. The expansion focuses on adding land, power and data centre shell capacity at sites designed to host multiple generations of NVIDIA DSX systems. Participating providers will operate the facilities, while NVIDIA will supply the DSX platform, computing systems, networking, software and ecosystem support. Demand for AI computing has risen as companies, researchers and public sector bodies seek more local access to large-scale infrastructure for training and deploying models. The broader buildout is intended to serve Australian startups, universities, researchers, developers, enterprises and AI-focused companies. NVIDIA also tied the expansion to broader use of its Nemotron open models in Australia, saying greater local access to computing resources and models would help organisations develop regional applications and agents for domestic industries. **Partner buildout** Several participating groups also outlined separate projects under the wider programme. Firmus is extending its Project Southgate initiative, which is intended to support demand from hyperscale operators and AI-focused customers in Australia and the Asia-Pacific region. “Project Southgate represents a tangible commitment to building Australia's AI future,” said Oliver Curtis, Co-Founder and Co-CEO of Firmus. “Together with NVIDIA, we are developing AI factories that will give Australian businesses, researchers and innovators access to world-class computing capacity at home, while positioning Australia to meet growing AI demand across Asia-Pacific,” Curtis said. Sharon AI is deploying up to 68,000 NVIDIA GPUs linked with NVIDIA Quantum InfiniBand and NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet networking. The infrastructure is intended to support startups, enterprises and research organisations. “Australia has the energy, connectivity and ambition to lead in AI. That potential only becomes real capability when organizations can access world-class compute without compromising on security or sovereignty,” said James Manning, Co-Founder and CEO of Sharon AI. “By building on NVIDIA's DSX platform, Sharon AI is equipped to bring gigawatt-scale AI factories to Australian enterprises, researchers, government and AI natives. With the trust and reliability needed to build, train and deploy AI at scale, Australia can turn its natural advantages into a genuine national AI capability,” Manning said. IREN is combining NVIDIA's DSX architecture with its own operations across power, land, data centres and GPU deployment. Infra & Chips.content: Posted: # AI infrastructure company Cornelis raises $205M to chip away at Nvidia’s dominance Cornelis, a company creating networking technology to help AI chips communicate more effectively, announced Monday that it has raised $205 million in a funding round led by IAG Capital Partners. It also announced a product called Active Compute Fabric, a network technology that targets the fact that much GPU time is wasted waiting for data to arrive. Cornelis hopes to address this with a networking fabric that lets chips process and send information at the same time. The company, which spun off from Intel in 2020, is competing with Nvidia by offering an open architecture, meaning customers can use a variety of GPU and accelerator hardware with Cornelis’ networking fabric. Though Nvidia chips can technically run on other networking fabrics, they’re optimized to run on Nvidia’s own software, making it much easier — and more enticing — for customers to use Nvidia’s full GPU stack. Cornelis is part of a new wave of AI infrastructure companies emerging to break apart Nvidia’s market dominance, piece by piece (or chip by chip, one could say). Cornelis hopes to address this with a networking fabric that lets chips process and send information at the same time. The company, which spun off from Intel in 2020, is competing with Nvidia by offering an open architecture, meaning customers can use a variety of GPU and accelerator hardware with Cornelis’ networking fabric. Though Nvidia chips can technically run on other networking fabrics, they’re optimized to run on Nvidia’s own software, making it much easier — and more enticing — for customers to use Nvidia’s full GPU stack. Cornelis is part of a new wave of AI infrastructure companies emerging to break apart Nvidia’s market dominance, piece by piece (or chip by chip, one could say). Cornelis has already started shipping its product and is working on a new generation of it, expected to be released later this year. Last day to book an exhibit table is September 18. Is It NVIDIA’s Hedge on Groq? * [AI Platforms](https://futurumgroup.com/category/ai-platforms/), [Data Center](https://futurumgroup.com/category/data-center/), [Hybrid Cloud & Infrastructure](https://futurumgroup.com/category/hybrid-cloud-infrastructure/), [Semiconductors, Supply Chain, & Emerging Tech](https://futurumgroup.com/category/semiconductors-supply-chain-emerging-tech/) ![d-Matrix Joins NVLink Fusion. Is It NVIDIA's Hedge on Groq?](https://futurumgroup.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/stock_0276.png) Analyst(s): Brendan Burke Publication Date: September 14, 2026 d-Matrix will integrate its Raptor inference XPUs into NVIDIA MGX racks through NVLink Fusion under a multi-year collaboration announced September 10. The deal follows Corsair deployments at Gimlet Labs and Parasail that proved out decode-phase acceleration alongside NVIDIA GPUs. Futurum examines whether Raptor’s 3D-DRAM architecture gives the NVIDIA ecosystem a frontier-scale hedge on the SRAM-based Groq 3 LPX. ## What Is Covered in This Article: * A multi-year d-Matrix and NVIDIA collaboration bringing Raptor XPUs into MGX racks through NVLink Fusion, alongside Vera CPUs, BlueField-4 DPUs, ConnectX-9 SuperNICs, and Spectrum-X networking. * A 144-XPU Raptor rack with 2.3 TB of 3D-DRAM capacity and 7.2 PB/s of memory bandwidth, projected at roughly 1,000 tokens per second per user on 3-trillion-parameter-class models at 1M context. * d-Matrix Corsair validation through Gimlet Labs speculative decoding results and Parasail’s heterogeneous prefill-decode deployment with NVIDIA GPUs * Raptor as a DRAM-based hedge on the SRAM-based Groq 3 LPX inside the NVIDIA inference platform. * ISCA 2026 early silicon data showing 4.71x higher throughput per card than HBM designs, with initial MGX availability expected Q4 2027. **The News:** d-Matrix announced a collaboration with NVIDIA that includes a multi-year product roadmap and brings d-Matrix XPUs into the NVIDIA AI factory ecosystem. As an NVLink Fusion partner, d-Matrix will integrate its next-generation Raptor inference XPUs into the latest NVIDIA MGX rack reference architecture, which features NVIDIA Vera CPUs, NVLink switches, BlueField-4 DPUs, ConnectX-9 SuperNICs, and Spectrum-X Ethernet networking. Astera Labs joins the effort with custom connectivity solutions. The rack targets ultra-low latency inference for AI labs, hyperscalers, and neoclouds offering premium token services, using heterogeneous disaggregation to split workloads between GPUs handling compute-intensive prefill and d-Matrix XPUs accelerating latency-sensitive decode. Raptor, the follow-on to the Corsair platform now in production, stacks a DRAM memory die and an SRAM compute die into a single package, is expected to tape out before the end of 2026, and is being evaluated at AI hyperscalers and frontier labs. Initial availability of Raptor XPUs in the NVIDIA MGX rack is expected in Q4 2027. ‘Being integrated into NVIDIA’s latest MGX rack-scale infrastructure with NVLink Fusion means our customers can deploy our inference XPUs alongside the broadly available NVIDIA AI factory platform,’ said Sid Sheth, Founder and CEO of d-Matrix. ## d-Matrix Joins NVLink Fusion. Infra & Chips.content: [Skip to content](#main) [![cio_africa_logo_white_](https://cioafrica.co/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/cio_africa_logo_white_.svg)](https://cioafrica.co/) [![cio_africa_logo_white_](https://cioafrica.co/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/cio_africa_logo_white_.svg)](https://cioafrica.co/) [Magazine](https://publications.cioafrica.co) [Radio](https://nohitsradio.live/) ###### advertisement [Artificial Intelligence (AI)](https://cioafrica.co/category/artificial-intelligence-ai/) [Egypt](https://cioafrica.co/category/egypt/) # Vodafone, Cassava Launch Egypt’s First AI Factory ![No photo available](https://cioafrica.co/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/no_photo.jpg)[![CIO Africa author](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/f28349c69d8f360fcda523920366623f?s=25&d=mm&r=g)](https://cioafrica.co/author/steve-mbego/)By[Steve Mbego](https://cioafrica.co/author/steve-mbego/) 3 min read The AI factory will provide a full-stack infrastructure environment for organisations and government agencies to develop and operate AI applications locally ![](https://cioafrica.co/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/ueidoalc.jpg) Vodafone Business and Cassava Technologies have partnered to develop Egypt’s first AI factory, creating sovereign AI infrastructure designed to enable local organisations to host, process and operate artificial intelligence applications within the country. The partnership will combine Vodafone Egypt’s enterprise capabilities with Cassava Technologies’ NVIDIA-powered cloud infrastructure to support government entities, businesses and other organisations seeking access to accelerated computing while keeping data within Egypt. Cassava Technologies is Africa’s first NVIDIA cloud partner. The collaboration will provide access to NVIDIA AI infrastructure through Vodafone Business, including GPU-as-a-Service, enabling organisations to deploy AI workloads for model training and inference at scale. ###### advertisement The companies said the initiative is intended to strengthen Egypt’s digital sovereignty, improve data protection and cybersecurity, and position the country as a regional hub for AI and advanced technology. Mahmoud El-Khatib, Vice President of Enterprise Business at Vodafone Egypt, said the partnership would strengthen the country’s AI infrastructure while supporting local data residency. “Our partnership with Cassava Technologies marks a pivotal step in Vodafone Egypt’s technology journey and reflects our continued commitment to investing in digital infrastructure that enhances Egypt’s readiness for advanced technologies.” ###### advertisement El-Khatib said the AI factory would provide organisations with access to advanced computing through GPU-as-a-Service, helping accelerate the adoption of AI while supporting Egypt’s digital economy and attracting investment in advanced technologies. Ahmed El Beheiry, Group Chief Technology & AI Officer and CEO of Cassava AI, said the partnership was aimed at enabling African businesses to move beyond being consumers of global technology. “For Cassava, contributing to building Egypt’s AI ecosystem is an act of empowerment, not just a technological milestone.” ###### advertisement He said the infrastructure would give Egyptian organisations the capacity to participate in global AI innovation while maintaining control over their data and technology environment. The AI factory will provide a full-stack infrastructure environment for organisations and government agencies to develop and operate AI applications locally. It will support local data hosting and processing while helping organisations meet regulatory and data residency requirements. The companies said the infrastructure could also help organisations strengthen cybersecurity, improve control over sensitive data and develop more efficient AI-powered products and services. The initiative comes as governments and businesses increasingly seek alternatives that complement conventional public cloud infrastructure with sovereign computing and AI-optimised cloud ser...
